headline_findings: This comparison covers two papers - one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper - each built from a different single source document, so the patterns described are specific to those two papers and not generalizable to either condition as a whole.

The Lyme disease paper centers on adverse events from antibiotic retreatment trials, while the Long COVID paper centers on employment and income disruption, so the two papers quantify almost entirely different kinds of burden with no overlapping dollar figures to compare directly.

Both papers independently flag that their key figures lack subgroup breakdown and that unresolved diagnostic or evidentiary gaps (no sensitive lab test for Lyme infection; no established diagnostic practice for Long COVID) undercut confident clinical or policy decisions.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports no out-of-pocket or any dollar cost figures at all; it is limited to trial-level clinical outcomes and adverse-event counts.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper describes patients facing higher insurance deductibles and costlier plans through participant quotes, but does not quantify these costs in dollar terms itself.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Readers looking for concrete out-of-pocket cost figures will not find quantified ones in either paper.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper contains no employment or income-loss data of any kind; its scope is confined to trial adverse events and efficacy signals.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper documents job loss, reduced hours, and income loss through patient narratives and cites external statistics including a 2022 U.S. national lost-wages estimate of $170,000,000,000 and figures such as 22% unable to work at 6 months and 45% requiring reduced schedules.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper addresses this dimension, so no cross-condition comparison of work/income burden is possible here.

comparison_rows.dimension: Diagnostic or evidentiary uncertainty underlying decisions

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper describes how, absent a sensitive lab test for active infection, treatment guidelines rest on four RCTs the authors argue were underpowered or misanalyzed, making 'no benefit' conclusions more contested than commonly presented.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper describes how the lack of established diagnostic practices makes it hard for patients to document functional limitations when applying for workplace accommodations.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers show that missing or contested diagnostic evidence shapes real-world decisions, even though the decisions themselves (treatment guidelines vs. workplace accommodations) differ.

comparison_rows.dimension: Access barriers (to treatment, benefits, or accommodations)

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not directly describe patient-facing access barriers; it implies that contested trial evidence underlies guideline restrictions on retreatment, but does not quantify any resulting access barrier.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper describes concrete access barriers, including difficulty obtaining disability benefits or workplace accommodations without objective diagnostic documentation.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Concrete, patient-facing access-barrier evidence appears only on the Long COVID side in these two papers.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports trial-level adverse-event rates for antibiotic retreatment, including a 10.91% significant adverse-event rate in the Krupp trial and an 18.92% adverse-event rate in the Fallon trial, with some events classified as serious (e.g., sepsis, anaphylaxis).

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper contains no data on treatment-related adverse events or iatrogenic harm.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Adverse-event/treatment-harm evidence appears only on the Lyme disease side in these two papers.

comparison_rows.dimension: How the burden may be undercounted by official or administrative data

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper does not discuss claims-based or administrative-data undercounting; its stated limitation is about contested trial evidence, not claims undercounting.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper flags that its cited 18% 'unable to return to work at 1 year' figure comes from New York workers' compensation claims data, an administrative source subject to coding and access-to-filing undercounting.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Only the Long COVID paper flags a specific claims-based undercounting mechanism in these two papers.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper leaves medical costs, productivity loss, care-utilization, long-term (beyond 6 months) outcomes, and population-level prevalence entirely unmeasured.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper leaves quantified per-patient medical costs, non-medical costs, productivity loss, and caregiver costs unmeasured by its own methodology, relying instead on qualitative themes and externally cited statistics.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Both papers leave a similar category of direct cost and productivity measurement unaddressed, despite covering very different aspects of burden.

lyme.finding: The Lyme disease paper reports its adverse-event figures as single pooled trial-arm numbers with no breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, or disability status.

long_covid.finding: The Long COVID paper reports its cited employment and wage-loss statistics as single pooled national/cohort figures with no subgroup breakdown.

comparison_rows.why_it_matters: Neither paper's key figures can be used to understand how burden varies across population subgroups.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers present their key figures as single pooled numbers without any breakdown by sex, age, race/ethnicity, disability status, or other subgroup.

evidence.note: The Krupp (6/55, 4 serious) and Fallon (18.9%, 7/37) adverse-event figures are reported as single pooled trial-arm numbers with no subgroup breakdown.
The cited $170 billion lost-wages estimate and the 22%/45%/18% employment-impact percentages are each single pooled national or cohort figures with no subgroup breakdown.

shared_themes.theme: Both papers point to a systemic evidentiary or diagnostic gap that undermines confident decision-making - in one case about treatment guidelines, in the other about accessing workplace accommodations.

evidence.note: Without a sensitive lab test for active infection, retreatment guidelines rest on four RCTs the authors argue were underpowered or improperly analyzed.
Lack of established diagnostic practices for Long COVID makes it hard for patients to document functional limitations when applying for workplace accommodations.

shared_themes.theme: Neither paper generates its own quantified dollar cost or productivity-loss figures; cost-related claims are either entirely absent or drawn from external citations rather than the paper's own data.

evidence.note: The paper reports no dollar costs, productivity loss, or insurance/access data anywhere; its focus is trial design and adverse events.
The only dollar figure present, $170,000,000,000 (2022), is a cited external estimate, not derived from this paper's own 21 interview participants.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Lyme disease paper quantifies treatment-related adverse-event rates from antibiotic retreatment trials, including serious events like sepsis and anaphylaxis, but these remain trial-level clinical safety figures rather than population-level cost burden.

evidence.note: Reports a 10.91% significant adverse-event rate in the Krupp trial and an 18.92% adverse-event rate in the Fallon trial, with serious events including sepsis and anaphylaxis.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper centers on employment disruption - job loss, reduced hours, income loss, and insurance disruption - documented through patient narratives and cited external statistics rather than the paper's own quantified data.

evidence.note: Describes job loss or change, reduced hours, loss of income, and costlier insurance plans through qualitative interview themes, alongside cited statistics like 22% unable to work at 6 months and 45% requiring reduced schedules.

condition_specific_themes.theme: The Long COVID paper explicitly flags that one of its cited employment statistics comes from an administrative claims source subject to undercounting.

evidence.note: The cited 18% 'unable to return to work at 1 year' figure comes from New York workers' compensation claims data, which is noted as subject to coding and filing-access undercounting.

evidence_gaps_shared: Neither paper reports direct medical or non-medical out-of-pocket cost figures generated from its own data.
Neither paper provides caregiver time or caregiving-cost data.
Neither paper offers population-level prevalence or incidence figures that would be needed to scale its findings to a broader population burden estimate.
cross_analysis.summary: This comparison covers exactly two papers - one Lyme disease paper focused on adverse events from antibiotic retreatment trials, and one Long COVID paper focused on employment and income disruption drawn from patient interviews and cited external statistics. The two papers address almost entirely different burden categories (iatrogenic harm versus employment), so there is little direct overlap to compare, but both independently note that their key figures lack subgroup breakdown and that unresolved diagnostic or evidentiary gaps complicate confident clinical or policy decisions. Numbers reported here are copied exactly as given in each paper's own figures, with their stated units and price years, and are not combined, averaged, or converted across papers. This analysis does not describe Lyme disease or Long COVID in general - it only reflects what these two specific uploaded documents report.
cross_analysis.limitations: This is a very small, non-random sample: exactly one Lyme disease paper and one Long COVID paper, with no papers covering both conditions and none in the unconfirmed category, as given in the real_stats counts (lyme: 1 paper; longCovid: 1 paper; cross: 0; other: 0). This is not a controlled study - the two papers were built from different source documents with different designs, populations, and purposes, so any pattern described here reflects only these two specific documents and should not be generalized to either condition as a whole.

learning_error: Learning card cites a figure that is not one of that paper's own: krupp_ae_rate

learning_cards.headline: Retreatment itself can cause harm worth measuring too
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Lyme disease paper reports an 18.92% adverse-event rate across both arms of the Fallon trial, with 85.71% of those events occurring in the ceftriaxone arm.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Long COVID paper does not report any adverse-event rate for its interventions or treatments.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could Long COVID treatment studies track and publish adverse-event rates comparable to the Fallon trial's reported figures?

learning_cards.headline: Work disability numbers show patients' daily life impact
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper cites a 66% disability share among patients and a 22% share unable to work at 6 months.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not report any employment or work-disability figures for retreatment trial participants.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Could future Lyme disease retreatment trials track participants' employment status before and after treatment?

learning_cards.headline: Reduced schedules and delayed return reveal hidden work costs
learning_cards.what_it_found: The Long COVID paper cites 45% requiring a reduced work schedule and 18% unable to return to work at 1 year in NY workers' compensation claims.
learning_cards.gap_on_other_side: The Lyme disease paper does not measure any work-schedule changes or return-to-work timelines for treated patients.
learning_cards.question_to_ask: Should Lyme disease treatment follow-up include measures of reduced work schedules or delayed return to work?

learning.takeaway: The Lyme disease paper could ask whether treatment harms are tracked as carefully as the Long COVID paper tracks work disruption, while the Long COVID paper could ask whether adverse events from its interventions are measured as clearly as the Lyme disease paper measures them.
